intro: Installing a wet room in a Cedarton home is one of the most significant bathroom upgrades you can make — and when it's done properly, it genuinely transforms how a bathroom looks, feels, and functions for years to come. But it's also a job where corners are commonly cut, and the consequences tend to show up months later behind tiles or under floors. In a market town like Cedarton, with its diverse mix of property ages and styles, getting the waterproofing and drainage right from the outset is everything. This guide walks you through what wet room installation actually involves here, what it costs, and what questions to ask before anyone starts lifting your floor.
localContext: Cedarton's housing stock creates a genuinely varied set of challenges for wet room installers. In older stone-built properties and period cottages — which make up a substantial portion of homes across the town — floors are rarely level, subfloor structures can be timber rather than concrete, and wall cavities may have quirks that a more modern home simply wouldn't present. Tanking systems need to be absolutely watertight in these settings, because water ingress into old stonework can cause serious structural damage over time. On the newer modern estates in and around Cedarton, concrete floors make the job more straightforward, but drainage positioning and underfloor heating integration still need careful planning. Cedarton also sits in a moderately hard water area, which means limescale build-up on screens, drains, and fixtures is a genuine long-term consideration — your installer should be specifying fittings and drainage designs that are practical to clean and maintain, not just attractive on the day.
serviceDetail: A proper wet room installation in Cedarton follows a clear sequence of stages, and understanding them helps you hold your installer to account. The process begins with a full survey of your existing bathroom space — checking the subfloor type, existing drainage position, pipe runs, and the structural integrity of walls. In period cottages particularly, this survey stage can uncover surprises, so any installer worth their salt will do this thoroughly before quoting. Once the design is agreed, the room is stripped back to the shell. For timber subfloors common in older Cedarton properties, a cement board or similar rigid substrate is laid to create a stable, waterproof-ready base. The floor is then graded — that is, given a precise slope toward the drain — which requires skill to get right, especially in rooms that aren't perfectly square. Full tanking follows: every surface is coated with waterproof membrane, with particular care given to corners and junctions where leaks are most likely to begin. The drain is installed and tested before any tiling begins. Tiles are then laid, grout applied, and all fixtures — shower valve, screen if required, lighting, and heated towel rail — are fitted and commissioned. A final check ensures all drainage runs freely and the room is fully sealed.
pricing: In Cedarton, wet room installations typically fall between £6,000 and £12,000 for a professionally completed project. The lower end applies to straightforward modern estate homes with concrete floors, simple layouts, and mid-range fittings. The higher end reflects the realities of period properties — complex subfloor work, bespoke tiling in irregular spaces, higher-end fixtures, and more labour time. Factors that push costs up include the need for structural reinforcement in older stone-built homes, underfloor heating installation, premium drain covers and shower valves, and large-format tiles that require a particularly flat and precisely graded floor. Always get a quote that separates labour, materials, and any contingency allowance — the surprises in older Cedarton properties are real, and a fixed-price quote with no contingency is often a warning sign.
whyLocal: Choosing an installer who knows Cedarton specifically makes a practical difference. Local tradespeople are familiar with the subfloor types common in the town's older stone-built and period properties, they understand building control expectations in East Sussex, and they have established relationships with local tile and bathroom suppliers — which can affect both lead times and pricing. There's also accountability: a local installer has a reputation to maintain in the same community where you live. When issues arise — and in wet room work, occasional snagging is normal — a local professional can return quickly rather than treating your job as an inconvenient journey.

faqs.q: Can a wet room be installed in an older period cottage in Cedarton?
faqs.a: Yes, but it requires more careful planning than a modern home. Timber subfloors need to be reinforced or overlaid with a rigid substrate before tanking, and irregular walls may need additional preparation. It's entirely achievable — many of Cedarton's older homes now have excellent wet rooms — but the survey stage is critical and the budget should reflect the extra complexity involved.

faqs.q: How long does wet room installation take in Cedarton?
faqs.a: Most wet room projects in Cedarton take between seven and fourteen working days from strip-out to completion. Older properties with subfloor complications or bespoke tiling requirements can push toward the longer end. Bear in mind that tanking and screed layers need drying time before tiling can begin, so some of that timeframe is unavoidable regardless of how quickly the team works.

faqs.q: Does hard water in Cedarton affect which fittings I should choose?
faqs.a: It's worth factoring in. Cedarton is in a moderately hard water area, so limescale will accumulate on chrome fittings, glass screens, and drain covers over time. Specifying easy-clean drain covers, quality shower valves with ceramic cartridges, and frameless or minimal-frame screens makes ongoing maintenance much more manageable. Your installer should be advising on this proactively.

faqs.q: Do I need building regulations approval for a wet room in Cedarton?
faqs.a: In most cases, a wet room replacement within an existing bathroom footprint doesn't require building regulations approval, though any electrical work — including heated floors or new lighting circuits — must be signed off by a Part P registered electrician. If you're altering drainage runs or creating a new bathroom space, building control may need to be notified. A reputable Cedarton installer will advise you on this before work begins.
